To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

Monte Carlo-derived conversion coefficients for the calculation of organ and effective dose from CTDI(W) are appropriate for the estimation of dose from spiral scans with pitch 0-1 and that separate sets of conversion coefficients for patients of different body size shall be derived.

the use of Monte-Carlo-derived normalized data for the estimation of CT patient dose is appropriate only when the body mass of the mathematical phantom and the CTDI(W) to CTDI(air) ratio of the scanner used in the Monte Carlo simulation are similar to the body mass of patient and the CTDIs of the specific scanner, respectively.

Monte Carlo-derived conversion coefficients may provide a good estimation of patient dose in CT examinations, but the accuracy of the results is dependent on the accuracy of the Monte Carlo data used.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the applicability and accuracy of Monte Carlo-derived data to provide accurate patient dose estimates for CT exposures.
the use of Monte-Carlo-derived normalized dose data to provide accurate estimates of patient dose from standard CT examinations.
the applicability and accuracy of Monte Carlo-derived data for the estimation of effective dose and organ dose in CT examinations.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
Monte Carlo-derived data are not suitable for patient dose estimation in CT examinations, unless the body size of patient and phantom is the same.
Monte Carlo-derived normalized dosimetric values are not appropriate for the estimation of organ doses and effective dose values from a specific CT examination performed on a particular scanner.
Monte Carlo simulation is an appropriate and accurate tool in patient CT dose assessment, but it is not yet an alternative for the experimental determination of CT dosimetric quantities.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

Monte Carlo simulation may provide a useful tool for the estimation of organ doses and patient dose from CT exposures, but its application requires a thorough understanding of the limitations of the methodology and a careful evaluation of the accuracy of the results.

Monte Carlo data derived from the simulation of standard patient CT examinations may be used for accurate estimation of patient dose only when: (a) the mathematical phantom used is similar to the body of the average adult patient, (b) the CT scanner used for the Monte Carlo simulation is similar to the scanner used for the CT examination, (c) the Monte Carlo data derived are appropriately modified for the specific scanner, and (d) the CT exposure is performed using the standard scanning protocol.
Monte Carlo simulation of CT exposures can be used for the calculation of dosimetric data for standard CT examinations performed on different CT scanners.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the application of Monte Carlo-derived conversion coefficients in patient dosimetry requires the use of appropriate data sets, which are scanner-specific and body-size specific.
Monte Carlo data should be used with care in the estimation of effective dose from CT examinations, since they may provide a significant inaccuracy if they are used inappropriately.

Monte Carlo-derived normalized dosimetric CT coefficients may be used to provide a good estimate of patient dose from helical CT examinations, provided that the patient body size is taken into account.
